Likeable Person Test Results: <1>What Your Score Actually Means</1>

You finished the test and you’re looking at a number. Maybe it’s higher than you expected, maybe it stung a bit. Either way, a percentage on its own doesn’t tell you much. This guide breaks down what every score range means in real terms, what each of the nine category scores is actually measuring, and — most importantly — what to do with the results so they become useful rather than just interesting.
Your Overall Score: <1>What the Number Tells You</1>

The overall percentage you see is a weighted average across nine social categories. It gives you a general sense of where you land, but here’s the thing — the headline number is the least useful part of your results. Two people can both score 68% and have completely different social profiles. One might be an excellent listener who’s unreliable with commitments. The other might be warm and dependable but terrible at conflict. Same score, very different people, very different fixes.
So read the overall score for general orientation, then immediately move to the category breakdown. That’s where the actual information lives.
🌟 Exceptional
Your social habits consistently create warmth and trust. People gravitate to you naturally.
😊 Excellent
Strong across the board. Minor rough edges, but they don’t define your interactions.
👍 Good
Solid likeability. Specific patterns hold you back from deeper connection.
🙂 Above Average
Most people find you pleasant. Deeper connections don’t form as easily as you’d like.
😐 Average
Surface-level interactions work fine. Specific habitual patterns create friction underneath.
Below 50%
💪 Needs Work
Clear barriers exist. Not a verdict — a starting point. Every single one is fixable.
Before You Worry: <1>The Liking Gap</1>
If your score was lower than you expected, there’s a piece of research you should know about before you spiral.

In 2018, researchers from Cornell, Harvard, Yale, and the University of Essex ran a series of experiments where strangers met and then rated two things: how much they liked the other person, and how much they thought the other person liked them. Across every experiment — short conversations, long conversations, month-long dormitory relationships — the same pattern appeared.
Research Finding — The Liking Gap

People consistently and significantly underestimated how much their conversation partners liked them. The researchers found that participants were “overly critical of themselves when judging their conversational performance” — and that this self-criticism was causing them to miss the positive social signals other people were sending. The gap was present across strangers and acquaintances, and persisted even after months of knowing someone.
<1>Boothby, E.J., Cooney, G., Sandstrom, G.M., & Clark, M.S. (2018). The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think? <2>Psychological Science, 29</2>(11), 1742–1756.</1>

What this means for your results: if you answered as your worst self — focusing on the times you were awkward, impatient, or distracted — rather than your actual average, your score may be deflated. It’s worth asking whether you answered honestly or pessimistically. They’re different things.
This doesn’t mean low scores are wrong. It means self-critical people should take their scores as a lower bound rather than a precise measurement.

Your 9 Category Scores: <1>What Each One Is Really Measuring</1>

This is the part most people skip — and it’s a mistake. Each category targets something specific, and a low score in one area tells you something very different from a low score in another. Here’s what you’re actually looking at in each one.
First Impressions
This measures the warmth you project in the first few minutes of meeting someone — whether you smile genuinely, remember and use names, and make people feel welcomed rather than assessed.
Low here? Research shows people form impressions in as little as seven seconds. Focus on eye contact and using someone’s name within the first 30 seconds of meeting them.
Communication

Whether you actually listen or just wait for your turn to talk. Whether you maintain eye contact. Whether people leave conversations feeling heard or subtly talked over. This category has outsized influence on every other social relationship you have.
Low here? Try pausing two full seconds before responding to anything. Then respond to what was specifically said — not to the general topic it reminded you of.
Positivity

Your general emotional tone and the atmosphere you create around you. This covers how often you compliment people, whether you express gratitude, and whether you tend to notice what’s wrong in a situation or what’s working.
Low here? Try one specific change: when someone tells you something good, be the first person to say something warm about it — before the conversation moves on. Timing matters in positivity.
Empathy

Whether you genuinely notice and respond to how other people are feeling — not just what they’re saying. This is one of the strongest individual predictors of likeability. People who score high here make others feel truly understood, which is rare and memorable.
Low here? Practice asking “how did that feel?” instead of immediately offering solutions or opinions. The question signals that you’re interested in their experience, not just the facts.
Emotional Intelligence

How you handle the difficult moments — disagreement, criticism, pressure, and situations where your buttons get pressed. A high score here means people feel safe being honest with you, which is the foundation of any real relationship.

Low here? The specific behaviour to work on: when someone criticises you, resist the urge to immediately explain or defend. Say “that’s useful — let me think about that.” You don’t have to agree. You just have to receive it without flinching.
Kindness

Whether you help people without being asked, share credit for things that went well, and celebrate others’ success without keeping score. Behavioural research from Dr. Travis Bradberry at TalentSmart found that highly likeable people score remarkably high on unprompted acts of kindness — things nobody asked them to do.
Low here? Pick one person this week and do something for them before they ask. Doesn’t have to be big. Just unprompted.
Reliability

Whether people can count on you. Not in the dramatic sense — in the small, consistent, everyday sense. Did you text when you said you would? Show up when you said you would? Finish what you said you’d finish? Trust is mostly built through these invisible moments, not the big ones.
Low here? For one month, don’t make a single commitment you don’t intend to keep. That includes casual “we should catch up soon” statements. Only say things you’ll follow through on.
Trustworthiness

Whether you’re honest, whether you gossip, and whether you take responsibility when you’re wrong. This category is the hardest to repair once damaged — which is why it’s worth paying close attention to even if your score here is just mediocre rather than low.
Low here? Start with the gossip. If you wouldn’t say something directly to the person, don’t say it. That single change shifts how people feel about you faster than almost anything else.
Social Skills

Your flexibility across different people, settings, and dynamics — whether you can read a room, adapt your register, find common ground with people different from you, and occasionally make people laugh without forcing it.

Low here? Focus on open-mindedness first. The next time someone holds a view you disagree with, spend 60 seconds asking questions about it before forming a counter-argument. This alone shifts how people experience you in conversation.
How to Actually <1>Use These Results</1>
Most people read their results, feel some feelings about them, and then don’t do anything different. That’s a waste of the most useful part of the exercise.
Here’s the approach that works:
Step 1: Find your floor, not your ceiling

Look at your lowest-scoring category. That’s where you start — not your second lowest, not the one you feel most comfortable working on. The lowest one. This matters because likeability categories are more interconnected than they look. Improving your worst area tends to pull up adjacent scores too. If Reliability is your floor, working on it will also improve Trustworthiness. If Communication is your floor, it’ll lift Empathy and Social Skills simultaneously.
Step 2: Choose one specific behaviour, not a vague intention

“Be a better listener” is not a behaviour. “Pause two seconds before responding to anything in conversation this week” is a behaviour. The difference matters because vague intentions don’t have a moment of accountability. You can’t tell, at the end of a conversation, whether you “were a better listener.” You can tell whether you paused before responding.
Each category description above gives you a specific starting behaviour. Pick the one that matches your lowest score.
“People are too busy forming negative thoughts about themselves to notice how much others like them.”
<1>— Erica Boothby, Cornell University, from the liking gap research (2018)</1>
Step 3: Run it for 30 days before evaluating

Don’t check in after a week and decide it’s not working. Social habits are slower to shift than we’d like, and the feedback from others is slower still. Commit to 30 days of one specific behaviour change, then retake the test. Most people who do this see meaningful movement — not just in their target category but in two or three others as a side effect.
⚠️ One mistake to avoid

Don’t try to improve all nine categories at once. It sounds efficient but it doesn’t work — because you end up being vaguely mindful of everything and specifically improving nothing. The research on behaviour change is consistent here: focused, specific practice beats broad awareness every time.
Step 4: Notice how people respond, not how you feel

Here’s something counterintuitive: the best evidence that your likeability is improving often comes from other people’s behaviour, not your own feelings. Do people seem more relaxed around you? Are conversations going longer than they used to? Is someone sharing more personal things with you? These are the actual signals. Your internal sense of “am I doing this right?” is a much less reliable indicator than paying attention to how other people are showing up differently.
A note on “spontaneous trait transference”

Research from Purdue University found a psychological phenomenon worth knowing about: when you say positive things about other people, observers unconsciously begin to associate those positive traits with you. In other words, talking about others generously makes you seem more generous. The reverse is also true. This is one of the fastest and most underrated likeability levers available to anyone at any score level.

What Your Score <1>Doesn’t</1> Mean
Before you go, it’s worth saying this plainly.

A low score on the <1>Likeable Person Test</1> doesn’t mean people find you unpleasant. It doesn’t mean your close relationships are in trouble. And it absolutely doesn’t mean you have some fundamental defect that makes you difficult to be around. What it means, specifically, is that certain habits you’ve developed over time — often without realising it — are creating friction in some of your social interactions.
Habits aren’t character. They’re patterns. Patterns change.

Also worth saying: the test is a self-report. It reflects how you see your own behaviour, which is not always how others see it. The liking gap research mentioned above suggests that most self-assessments lean pessimistic. If you answered during a bad week, after a difficult social situation, or while generally feeling low — your results will reflect that, not your actual average.
None of this means you should dismiss a low score. The categories that score low are almost always worth looking at. But approach them as a compass, not a verdict.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is a good score on the Likeable Person Test?

Above 70% is generally good. Scores in the 70–79% range mean your likeability is solid with some specific areas worth developing. Above 80% reflects genuinely strong social habits. But more useful than the headline number is your lowest category score — that’s where the most actionable information is, regardless of what your overall percentage looks like.
What does a low Likeable Person Test score mean?

It means specific social habits are creating friction — not that you’re fundamentally unlikeable. Look at which categories scored lowest rather than fixating on the overall number. And bear in mind the liking gap research: self-critical people consistently underestimate their actual likeability. A low score is a starting point for targeted improvement, not a final assessment of your social worth.
Which category should I focus on improving first?

Your lowest-scoring category, always. Not your most comfortable one to work on — your actual lowest. That said, if Trustworthiness or Reliability scored particularly low, prioritise those even if something else is technically lower. Trust takes longer to rebuild than communication style, so the sooner you start, the better.
Can I retake the test to track my progress?

Yes — and it’s a good idea to wait at least 30 days before doing so. Work on one specific behaviour change in your lowest category for a month, then retake it. Most people see improvement in more than one category because the skills are interconnected. Better listening habits, for example, tend to lift Communication, Empathy, and Social Skills simultaneously.
Why did I score lower than I expected?

Two likely reasons. First, you may have answered as your aspirational self rather than your actual everyday behaviour. Second, the liking gap research shows that self-critical and anxious people consistently rate themselves as less likeable than others actually find them. If your score felt harsher than your social life suggests it should be, consider retaking it and answering a bit more generously — not dishonestly, just without the extra layer of self-criticism.
